name: NakedPak board read

parts.title: Lettering
parts.intro: Where the word is the picture. Five languages, from heavy soft display type to copy set as the whole surface.

parts.title: Illustration
parts.intro: The drawn image. Five languages that differ in line, fill, and what the drawing is for.

parts.title: Photography
parts.intro: The made image. Four languages that differ in distance, light and what is allowed into the frame.

parts.title: The pack
parts.intro: Devices, materials and structure. Four languages carried by the object itself.

languages.title: Heavy soft display type
languages.definition: Cooper-style soft serifs, rounded sans and bubble letters: heavy, soft-edged, often touching, often larger than the panel that holds them.
reading: The weight carries the appetite. Strokes thicken toward the middle of the letter as if filled, counters shrink to slits, terminals round off. Yellowbird's mark (229) climbs and leans so the word seems to be getting up; Bezi's (083) is stretched to fit the lid of its tub until the letters are the container. When the letters sag, as in Dally's wordmark (063) beside its translucent peach spheres, the lettering is doing what the food does.

The lineage runs from Cooper Black (1922) through its second life on 1960s and 70s record sleeves and supermarket shelves, and the board's version keeps that warmth without the distress: flat color, clean edges, a single offset outline at most (141). Where the letters are geometric and rounded rather than serifed (006, 010, 024, 125), the reference shifts a decade later, to the bubble lettering of children's television and cereal.

The relationship to the pack is the point. These marks are set large enough to be cropped by the panel (046, 108, 116), so the pack becomes a window onto a bigger word. The food, when it appears, sits below or behind. The letter is the hero and the product is the evidence.

plates.caption: The mark climbs. Letters lean into each other and the baseline rises, so the word reads as a motion, not a label.
Lettering stretched to the lid's edge. The name becomes the container's shape; three colorways change nothing else.
The stems sag. Beside see-through jelly spheres, the letters take on the product's physics.
A soft serif alone on a field, pale blue on red. Nothing else is needed; the type is the poster.
Giant warped letters in one green on another, filling the panel. The carton is a crop of a word.
Fat serif with an offset second color, printed slightly off-register. The warmth comes from the print, not from distress.

languages.relations: Pairs with the label register (L03) at small scale. Opposes the reductive pack (L18). The heavy soft letter and the character (L09) are the board's two most common signs of warmth, and they rarely appear together.

languages.title: Script lettering
languages.definition: Joined or brush-made lettering that carries a human hand: monoline, casual script, heavy upright script, swash.
reading: Script is the board's second voice. It almost never carries the whole message; it sits over or beside a plainer face and supplies the tone. Lazy Sundays (150) puts a looping "Lazy" over fat rounded caps. Risotto (243) sets the product name in script above a bowl. Nooish (226) uses "Instant Classic!" in script as the aside inside a layout of bands. The script is the parenthesis.

Three sources are visible. The sign-painter's monoline (016, 155, 119) is quick and even, a brush that never stops. The soda-fountain script (228, 194) is heavier, upright and joined, a quotation of 1950s American refreshment. The hand-lettered display script (053, 009) has swash and swelling, closer to 1970s phototype. Which one a brand chooses sets its decade.

Because script implies a person writing, it does the work of a signature. Stiller's runs it up the can like a wall sign; SuperRico (016) is nothing but the script on red, which is enough to be a brand.

plates.caption: Monoline script alone on red. One stroke width, one color; the brand is a signature.
Looping script laid over heavy rounded caps. The two faces split the job: mood above, name below.
Upright joined script with a registered mark. The 1950s fountain sign, quoted exactly.
Swash script that fits the pastry's rounded panel. Pink, sprinkles and script agree on one era.
Script over a photograph of the plate and gingham. The lettering is the restaurant's sign.
Script name over a bowl seen from above, color per flavor. Script here is warmth; the bowl is the fact.

languages.relations: Usually paired with L03 (condensed caps) as the quieter voice. Belongs to the same quotation habit as the grocery vernacular (L15).

languages.title: Condensed caps and label typography
languages.definition: Narrow capitals and small typographic furniture: the voice of the tin label, the notice and the specimen sheet.
reading: This is where facts live. Wood-type gothics and condensed grotesks carry flavor names (025, 034, 291), while small caps, typewriter and mono carry weight, count and origin (162, 305, 045). The register reads as honest because it is the type of things that are not designed: crate labels, price notices, specification sheets.

It has a poster mode too. The condensed serif stack (011, 139) sets a pep-talk sentence in a block, black on yellow, and the repetition of words becomes the rhythm of the image. Glossier's bodega notice (120) is the same idea in one ink on pink. The copy is plain; the setting makes it a picture.

Within a pack, this register is what makes the heavy soft display type (L01) legible as a brand. Juicy Marbles (291) sets "meat" enormous and the grams small; Heyday (301) sets the whole name in it and lets color do the rest. The difference between a loud pack and a quiet one on this board is mostly how much of the panel is given to this voice.

plates.caption: A sentence stacked in condensed serif, black on yellow. Repetition makes the rhythm; the words are the image.
Condensed sans cropped by the carton's foot, one color per flavor. The crop implies the word continues below.
One word set huge in a heavy grotesk, the grams small beside it. Hierarchy by scale, nothing else.
Dense label typography: bilingual caps, rules, a tiger, numbers. The crowded label as a mark of authenticity.
One ink, condensed caps, left-aligned. The corner-store notice as a brand announcement.
A 1970s wordmark over typewriter text. The specimen sheet as stationery.

languages.relations: The counterweight to L01 and L02 on nearly every pack. The grocery vernacular (L15) is this register's furniture.

languages.title: Copy-led design
languages.definition: A sentence set as the whole surface: the pep-talk poster, the talking pack, the billboard that says one thing.
reading: A group of pins has no image except what the words say. "Have a really, really nice day" (011), "Good things happen when you try" (139), "Let's make things better" (122): second-person encouragement, set large, in a face that softens it. The lineage is the 1970s head-shop poster and the greeting card, and the tone is kind rather than clever.

On packs the same idea turns into a voice. Lazy Food (256, 257) repeats CHEESY behind its pouch and names itself for the effort it saves; Oatly (167) covers its carton in talk; Matty's (232) quotes its own instructions as if a friend were speaking. The pack addresses the buyer directly and the design steps back to let it.

What makes these work is restraint elsewhere. One face, one or two colors, and a sentence short enough to read from across a room (225, 264). When the copy has to share the surface with a photograph (302, 253), the letters are cut out or laid on as objects, so that the sentence stays a thing rather than a caption.

plates.caption: A promise in condensed serif on yellow. No product, no image; the sentence is the poster.
The pouch in front of its own adjective, repeated. The pack is the talker and the room is its speech.
Outline hand lettering, green on cream. Encouragement at the scale of a wall.
Cut-paper letters laid on a table photograph among hands. The sentence is set on the dinner, not over it.
Copy covers the carton. The pack reads like a letter.
A billboard that says one thing about the product and nothing about the brand.

languages.relations: Shares its faces with L03 and L01. Where L04 meets photography (302, 253) it borrows the cut-paper method of L08.

languages.title: Type integrated with the food
languages.definition: Type set in, on or as the food: letters made of liquid, words fitted to a fruit, a title that frames the dish.
reading: Here the two halves of a pack, word and picture, become one thing. TOMATO (094) is set in a thin wide serif directly on a macro of sauce, so the word is read through the texture. BUBBLES (114) is spelled in water. Algae Cooking Club (134) is written in oil on steel. The letters stop being a label and become a property of the food.

A second version fits the word to the food's silhouette. Happy Chuseok (009) is drawn inside a fruit; NOMM (152) puts its letters inside a rolling pin and bowls; the SOUP ladle (158) pours its own name. These are rebus devices from sign painting and the 1960s poster, and they read fast because the shape is recognized before the word.

The third version uses the word as a frame. Lazy Nights (280, 336) sets its name enormous down the side of a noodle photograph; Dippa (290) weaves giant cream letters behind a figure and in front of a bowl. The type is architecture and the food lives inside it. This is the most promising of the three for a product that has one action to show.

plates.caption: A wide thin serif set on the sauce itself. The word is read through the texture; the texture is the field.
Letters formed from water on blue. Type as the material.
Letters inside a rolling pin and bowls, two colors. A rebus: the kitchen spells the sound of eating.
The ladle pours its own word. Stipple engraving, the 1890s trade card.
The name runs down the side at the scale of the frame. The noodles are inside the word.
Giant letters behind the person and in front of the bowl. Type and photograph in one space.

languages.relations: Needs photography (L11) or illustration (L06) to exist. Opposes the reductive pack (L18), where type never touches the image.

languages.title: Two-color spot illustration
languages.definition: One line weight, one or two flat inks, halftone or stipple for tone. The drawing of the mid-century cookbook and the instruction leaflet.
reading: This is the printed kitchen. Numbered steps drawn in pink and green (076), a red pot on green tile cut in lino (137, 153), stacked enamel pots in a folk pattern (077), a sandwich exploded into floating layers (095). The line is even and unhurried, the fills are flat, and shading, where there is any, is a screen of dots. The reference is the two-color spot illustration of 1950s cookbooks and the process diagrams on the back of a box.

The pot is a token of this language rather than a subject. Drawn this way it signals the domestic kitchen of a particular era: enamel, flowers, steam as a curl. When the type is hand-carved to match (137), the whole image reads as one print. Graza's man and olive (132) do the same in the register of a 1940s newspaper ad.

What the language does to tone: it makes instruction friendly. The same steps set in photographs would be a manual; drawn in two inks they are an invitation. It also keeps the food generic (a tomato, a pot), which is why the brands on the board pair it with a photograph when the food itself needs to be seen.

plates.caption: Six numbered steps in pink and green, halftone fills. Instruction drawn as a cookbook spot.
A red pot on green tile, hand-carved letters. One print, one kitchen.
Enamel pots stacked, each with its own folk pattern, steam as a curl. The pot as an ornament of the home.
A sandwich exploded into floating layers, two-color halftone. The diagram as a picture.
A pouch drawn like a 1940s ad: man, olive, small type, lime green. The drawing supplies the era.
Bowls as a two-color pattern. The drawn object repeated until it is a textile.

languages.relations: The natural partner of L03 for instructions. Its opposite in illustration is botanical realism (L07): same subjects, different claim.

languages.title: Botanical illustration
languages.definition: Produce painted or drawn as a specimen: watercolor, gouache, engraving. The seed packet and the horticultural plate.
reading: A tomato cut in half in watercolor (330), heirlooms in a loose gouache (098), a radish on a kraft packet (203) and the same radish embroidered (204). The drawing attends to the particular fruit, its skin and seeds, with the care of a catalog. The reference is the seed packet, the canning label with a painted beet (185) and the botanical plate.

The claim this makes is about the ingredient, not the brand: this is what goes in. It is the opposite of the spot drawing (L06), which keeps food generic. Fond's label (185) shows how it sits inside a pack: the painting at the center, bands and gold rules around it, the typographic furniture of the 1940s grocer.
The register is slow. It reads well on a single pack and in print, less well as a system, which is why it appears on the board mostly as single pins rather than as ranges.

plates.caption: A tomato in section, watercolor. Seeds, gel and skin described one at a time.
Heirloom tomatoes and an onion in loose gouache on paper. The catalog plate, warmed.
A radish on a kraft seed packet. The packet is the oldest ingredient-forward pack there is.
A painted beet inside bands and gold rules. The 1940s canning label done with care.
The radish embroidered. The same image carried by a different craft.
Figs drawn on a pasta box for a limited edition. Realism as the sign of a season.

languages.relations: Opposes L06 in its claim. Belongs with the grocery vernacular (L15) when it sits inside a label.

languages.title: Cut-paper illustration
languages.definition: Flat shapes with no outline. Color does the modeling. After Matisse's cut-outs, through the mid-century poster.
reading: The cookbook cover Food & More Food (001) is the clearest case. Five hands in five flat colors reach for a chili, a tomato and a leek; the fingers get one soft spray of shadow and nothing else. Black marker squiggles run between the hands and off the cover onto the backdrop. The title is a stacked geometric display face with sliced counters, set as a solid block in the lower right. Three registers are at work: the cut shape, which is gestural and warm; the marker line, which is quick and personal; and the architectural type, which holds still while everything else moves. The image is convivial because the hands are many and reaching, and it is legible because the type refuses to join in.

Lentiful (218, 219) uses the same method as a system: vegetables cut from flat color, laid on a band of flavor color, repeated across a range. Mmm (250) sets cut leaves on dark green under a word. Oxente (002, 310) reduces produce to one-ink silhouettes and makes them a pattern. The cut shape is quick to read, cheap to print, and survives at any size, which is why it travels from poster to pouch without changing.
The language is cheerful by construction. Without outlines there is no drawing to be good or bad at; the color relationships do all the work, and strong, simple contrasts read as optimism.

plates.caption: Five flat hands, one airbrushed cue of volume each, marker squiggles escaping the cover, a block of geometric type. Three registers in one image.
Cut leaves and vegetables on dark green under a word. Matisse at the scale of a poster.
Cut produce laid along a color band, repeated across a range. The method becomes a system.
Produce as one-ink silhouettes on red. The cut shape as pattern.
Letters cut as tiles that interlock into a square. Lettering handled as paper.
Pastel pouches with a giant white grotesk at the foot and one tiny cut-out ingredient. The method at its smallest.

languages.relations: Shares a lineage with L06 but refuses the line. Where the figure gets a face it becomes L09.

languages.title: Character illustration
languages.definition: A cast that performs the food: rubber-hose mascots at one end, naive one-line vegetables at the other.
reading: The board carries two character traditions and they make opposite claims. The rubber-hose mascot (007, 212, 319) is polished: round limbs, gloves, a grin, the 1930s cartoon that became the standard of American food advertising. It promises craft and a brand with a history. The naive vegetable (206, 208, 151) is one line, one color, barely a face; it promises sincerity and a brand that does not take itself seriously.

The interesting work is in the middle. Long Weekend (043, 165, 182) puts a photograph of the soup in a frame and lets cartoon vegetables walk around it, so the photo is a window in a cartoon world. Then it reverses the trick (251, 164): an onion character lounges in the real cup with real water poured on it. The drawing sits on the photograph like a sticker, never entering its space, and that refusal is the joke. Bowl'd (241) makes the cast a system, one vegetable per tile, one tile per flavor.

What a character does to a pack is set its audience. The more finished the drawing, the more it reads as for children or as nostalgia for having been one. The looser the line, the more it reads as an aside between adults.

plates.caption: A rubber-hose boy with a bowl, yellow and blue. The 1930s cartoon as a record label.
A cow and a sun with faces, drawn in the flavor's darker tone, on a chocolate-shell cup. The cast tells the farming story.
Six tiles, six vegetables with faces, one per flavor. The character as a sorting system.
A photograph framed inside a green card, cartoon vegetables walking around it. The photo is a window in a drawn world.
A drawn onion lounging in a real cup while real water pours in. The drawing stays a sticker on the photograph.
Vegetables in a bowl, one line, one color. Barely a face, and that is the charm.

languages.relations: Overlaps with macro photography (L11) in the hybrids (251, 164, 089). The character and heavy soft display type (L01) seldom share a panel.

languages.title: Psychedelic collage and retro print
languages.definition: Cut photographs, airbrush, chrome, halftone and off-register ink: images that are about a printed past.
reading: Pasta Dreams (091) is the fullest example. Photographic cut-outs of spaghetti, breadsticks, a tomato and a chili are arranged on a sky of clouds and orange swirls; a fork lifts a nest of pasta over a checkerboard floor; bubbles drift. The lettering is a 1970s bubble script. The sensibility is specific: the cut-out animation of Terry Gilliam, the Italian-kitsch advertising of the 1970s, food made monumental and placed on a stage. It is camp with appetite, and the collage is what makes the appetite theatrical rather than documentary.

Around it sit the other retro prints. Chrome bubbles on a dark field (113) and the Dior card (014) are 1980s airbrush. Oh What Fun (138) is a 1960s greeting card with drop shadows and sparkles. Brilliant (021) is Pop's detergent box in four colorways. Vybes (081) marbles fruit like endpaper. Strangers (105) blurs its color into soft blobs. These share a wish to look printed, or filmed, in a decade other than this one.

The register is the most purely nostalgic on the board, and the most dangerous for a new product: it tells you what era the brand admires before it tells you what the product is. On the board it belongs to posters, title cards and limited editions, almost never to a shelf pack.

plates.caption: Photographic cut-outs on a painted sky, a fork over a checkerboard, a 1970s bubble script. Food as surreal theatre.
Chrome bubbles on a dark-to-orange field. 1980s airbrush, kept for the bubbles rising.
Red letters with drop shadows and sparkles on green stripes. A 1960s greeting card.
A detergent-box burst in four colorways. Pop's supermarket, rebuilt as a candy range.
Clipped collage cards on coffee bags. Collage as a label.
Color blurred into soft blobs on black boxes. The printed past as an out-of-focus memory.

languages.relations: The most self-aware of the languages. Its textures (riso, halftone, misregister) appear quietly inside L01 and L06 without the nostalgia.

languages.title: Macro texture and the drawn overlay
languages.definition: Food photographed close enough to become a surface. Then, in a few pins, a drawn line laid on that surface.
reading: At this distance the food stops being a dish and becomes a material: noodles filling the frame (096), stew with beads of oil (097), cherries in ice (101), a bitten pastry with sprinkles (196). The language of appetite in contemporary food photography is texture at macro, and the board collects it without packs attached. Nine broth cups from above (184) take the same interest and turn it into a typology: foam, oil, a lemon wheel, each cup a different surface.

The hybrids are where this becomes useful. TOMATO (094) sets thin type on a sauce macro. The tomato purée with a tiny drawn hand (089) does something stranger: the texture supplies seriousness and hunger, the line drawing supplies scale play and a shrug. The drawing sits on top like a sticker and refuses to be in the photograph's space, so the image is affectionate rather than gourmet. Broth with handwritten ingredient labels (133) and mac and cheese with round stickers (294) do the same with words. The combination lets a brand be appetizing and light at once, which neither register manages alone.
The cost is clarity about the product. Macro texture is generic by nature; without a pack or a line, a noodle macro belongs to anyone.

plates.caption: Stew close enough to see the oil bead. The food as a surface; no pack, no plate.
Nine cups from above, each a different surface. Texture arranged as a typology.
A macro of tomato purée with a small drawn hand. Appetite from the texture, a shrug from the line.
Broth with the ingredients handwritten onto it. The photograph annotated.
Mac and cheese filling the frame, round stickers on top. The pack's furniture on the food.
A bitten pastry on red, sprinkles sharp. The crop makes a dessert into a pattern.

languages.relations: The hybrids join this language to L09 (characters) and L05 (the word in the food). The color-field set (L12) is its opposite in distance.

languages.title: Color-field product photography
languages.definition: The pack on a stage of one color, hard light, one shadow. From a single hero to a family tiled across the frame.
reading: This is the studio language of the 2010s and 20s: a pack set on seamless paper in one color, lit hard from one side so it throws a single shadow, the room matched to the pack (047, 224: red cups, red tomatoes, red wall). Sometimes the room is a floor of tile (092, 300, 314) or a gradient (064, 260). The product becomes a sculpture and the color becomes the mood.

Within this language the main variable is number. Nufs alone on sky blue (064) is a monument. Ollie's pair (033, 107) is a conversation. Nooish's cups laid in rows on a slant (254) and Pick Up's wall of boxes (022) are a pattern, the supermarket shelf-blocking rebuilt as a picture. The nine broth cups (184) take the idea to a typology, where the arrangement matters more than any single object.

The language favors brands with a color-per-flavor system, because the set can change with the pack. It is also where most of the board's monochrome pins live: one hue over pack, prop and ground reads as control, and control reads as a brand.

plates.caption: One box on sky blue with salt scattered, hard light. The pack as a monument.
Red cups, red tomatoes, red cloth, red wall. One hue is the whole set.
Cups laid in rows on a slant, cropped. The range as a pattern.
Boxes tiled edge to edge in three primaries. Shelf-blocking as a picture.
Cans grouped on blue tile against a red wall. A kitchen built as a color field.
Three boxes in three rooms, each matched to its own color. The system shown as a set of sets.

languages.relations: Hosts most of the color-per-flavor systems. Opposes the kitchen table (L13), where the set is a real room.

languages.title: Ingredient still life
languages.definition: The pack among its raw ingredients, in a real or convincing room: the plinth of garlic, the tomato on the can, the lunch table.
reading: Where the color-field set controls everything, this language lets the room in. A hummus tub on a heap of garlic against yellow tile (247). A tomato balanced on a pair of bone-broth cans (186). A mayonnaise bottle on a plate with pickles and dill (263). Lentil cups on a table with the beans and peppers that went into them (221). The ingredient is placed beside the pack as evidence, and the light is warmer and softer than in the studio.

The composition is the still life: a few objects, a surface, a cloth. It reads as editorial rather than retail, and brands use it for the feed and the billboard rather than the shelf. The ramen bowl on red tile with a sachet beside it (166) and the lunch on a striped tablecloth (258) show how far the pack can recede before the picture stops being about it.
The claim is simple and strong: this is food, here is what is in it. For a product whose contents are the point, this is the language that proves them.

plates.caption: A tub on a heap of garlic, yellow tile behind. The ingredient as a plinth.
A tomato balanced on two cans. The contents, placed on top of the container.
A bottle laid on a plate with pickles and dill, on tile. The pack as one object on a table.
Cups among the beans, peppers and onions that fill them. Evidence arranged around the product.
A bowl on red tile with chilies and a sachet. The pack almost disappears into the meal.
A tin on a bed of olives, in soft light. Pack and ingredient share the color.

languages.relations: Opposes L12 in control. Shares the ingredient-as-evidence claim with botanical realism (L07).

languages.title: Demonstration photography
languages.definition: A hand, a pour, a drop, a dissolve. The product shown doing the thing it does.
reading: Cometeer (315, 316) is the clearest brand built on this language. A dark puck sinks in a glass mug in hard light; a hand tips a capsule over a mug. The photograph explains a product no one has seen before, and the brand is the explanation. The puck held between finger and thumb (313) and a bean in tweezers (271) extend it: single objects shown as if in a lab, lit like jewelry.

The rest of the board uses the hand more casually. A hand holds the pouch on an open palm (108, 297, 170); a spoon lifts from a cup (220, 249); a woman squeezes mayo at the open fridge (259); a child pours olive oil (326). These are not demonstrations so much as proofs of use: someone is eating this, now.

The pour and the drop are the board's images of transformation, and there are few of them: a rope of soda into a glass (268), water falling onto a cartoon onion (251), and the two dissolves. For a product whose point is that it goes into the pot, this is the thinnest language on the board and the most important.

plates.caption: A puck sinking in a glass mug, hard light, a two-color ground. The product explained in one picture.
A capsule tipped into a glass of ice. The pour as the brand's only gesture.
A puck between finger and thumb against a gradient. The lab object shot as jewelry.
A spoon lifted from a cup held in both hands. Proof of use, not demonstration.
A woman squeezing mayo at the open fridge. The product in the middle of a life.
Soda falling as a rope into a glass of ice. The pour as refreshment, from the 1950s.

languages.relations: Needs the macro (L11) or the set (L12) as its ground. The hybrids (251) are a demonstration with a cartoon in it.

languages.title: Grocery vernacular devices
languages.definition: The supermarket's own furniture, quoted: bursts, ovals, seals, price stickers, bands and gold rules.
reading: A third of the board carries something that looks stuck on afterward. A "Yes!" sticker on an apple (169), three Hato ovals in three colorways (211), a navy burst on a can, a painted tray of tomatoes with its price labels (193). These are not decoration; they are the grammar of the grocery store, and using it is a way of claiming a place on the shelf before the pack is on one.

Two generations are visible. The older one is the label: Heyday's cans (222, 223) and Fond (185) rebuild the 1940s canning label with bands, seals and a painted ingredient; Nooish (226) does it with a bowl window and "Instant Classic!"; Ramen is Love (341) is a 1950s Japanese-American wrapper. The newer one is the sticker: a claim in a pill, a burst or a cloud, tilted, as if applied by a person (231, 293). The first says we have always been here; the second says we just arrived and we are friendly.
The vernacular is where the voice of the tin label (L03) gets its shapes. It is also the easiest language on the board to overdo: once a pack has four bursts it is a coupon.

plates.caption: Cans stacked in a tile kitchen, labels in bands with seals. The 1940s canning label, rebuilt.
A sticker on an apple. The produce label as a brand mark.
One oval, three colorways. The badge as the whole identity.
A supermarket tray of tomatoes painted with its price stickers. The vernacular made into a picture.
Bands, a bowl window, a script aside. The instant-soup label with its grammar intact.
Stickers on a photographed pepper over a type pattern. The claim as something a person stuck on.

languages.relations: Supplies the shapes for L03's register. Shares the quotation habit with script (L02) and the retro print (L10).

languages.title: Translucency and windows
languages.definition: Seeing the food through the pack: die-cut windows, clear bags, frosted film, jelly, a sheet held to the light.
reading: The board wants to see inside. Dally's pouch (063) is white with the peach jelly spheres showing through. Lumi's wrapper (100) cuts a window around the candy. Onigiri (174) is wrapped in printed film with the rice visible. Rocca (324) sets translucent jelly shapes into a gray box like gems. A sachet of blooming tea shows the flower through a round window (178).

Then there are the material pins, which have no brand at all: a clear, seed-flecked sheet in two hands (331), leaves sealed in an edible film (332), tinted translucent sheets cut by hand (177). These are the closest things on the board to the product itself, and they are photographed as objects of wonder rather than as packaging.

Translucency is a claim of trust by sight, and it is also an aesthetic: the sugared jelly cubes (197, 198) and the frosted pouches (109) glow because light passes through them. A language that works best when the food is beautiful and worst when it is not.

plates.caption: A clear sheet flecked with seeds, held in two hands. The material as the whole image.
A white pouch, the peach spheres showing through. The window is most of the front.
Onigiri in printed film with the rice visible. The wrapper that shows and tells at once.
Translucent jelly shapes set into a gray box. Candy presented as gems.
Sugared jelly cubes with long shadows. Light passes through the food.
Leaves sealed in an edible sheet. The wrapper and the food are one object.

languages.relations: The only language on the board that touches the product's own material. Opposes the printed carton of L17.

languages.title: Structural and conceptual packaging
languages.definition: Structure that means something: a carton drawn as an oven, a box that folds into a tray, a lid printed on the inside.
reading: A box printed as an oven with cartons stacked inside it (115). A line of microwave boxes with the timer at 1:30 (190). A seed box that folds into its own husk tray (322). A T-shirt sold in a cereal box with a word search on the back (118). These packs are jokes about packs, and the lineage is Pop: Warhol's Brillo boxes made the supermarket carton a sculpture, and these make the carton a prop.

A quieter version prints the inside. Graza's mailers (325, 327) carry a drawing and a line on the inner lid. Basao's tea sachets are filed in a kraft box like index cards (333). Blooming tea (178, 180) sells a box with a window and a glass teapot beside it. The structure does the storytelling and the outer graphics can stay plain.

Pick Up's back panel (283), "collect all six flavors" with a how-to-enjoy strip, is the cereal box's own grammar reused on a biscuit. The pack as a thing to read, keep or play with is a different promise from the pack as a sign, and it is the one that survives the unboxing.

languages.title: Reductive packaging
languages.definition: Minimal surface, small type, plain material. The pack that lets the object or the material speak.
reading: A green coffee pouch with a tiny white label (109). White pet-food sachets with a line drawing and nothing else (285). An apricot and a pear on gray with three spaced words, FOOD AS ART (093, 117). A can of tomatoes held in a hand, unbranded (191). These pins are the board's quiet, and they are quiet by subtraction: no burst, no character, no color field.

Two sources: the specialty-coffee pouch, which inherited its reticence from Japanese stationery, and the still-life photograph of the museum catalog. Both ask the viewer to look at the thing rather than the sign. Rose's boxes (303, 235) belong here too: a pattern taken from the food, an emboss, and type small enough to be missed.

The language is a position. On a shelf of heavy display type and bursts, the plain pack reads as expensive, and the material (kraft, frosted film, uncoated board) has to be good enough to carry that reading.

tensions.title: Appetite and flatness

plates.caption: Stew at macro: the food as a surface.
A pot in lino: the food as a sign.
The join: texture under a drawn line.

text: Photography at close range promises taste; the two-color drawing promises charm. The board wants both, and most packs choose one per panel: a photograph on the front, a drawing on the back. The hybrids (089, 251, 133) put them in one image, and they only work because the drawing refuses to enter the photograph's space. It stays a sticker, a scale joke, a note. The moment the line tries to model the food, the two registers fight.

What is interesting is what each loses. The macro loses the product (noodles belong to no one); the drawing loses the hunger (a pot is a pot). A pack that needs both has to decide which one is the ground and which one is the remark.

tensions.title: The quoted label and the new voice

plates.caption: Heyday: the 1940s canning label, straight.
Sorry Nonna: the same tradition, apologizing.
Lazy Food: no tradition, just the voice.

text: Nostalgia on the board arrives two ways: as a straight quotation of an old grammar (Heyday, Fond, Stiller's) and as a joke told inside that grammar (Sorry Nonna, Nooish's "Instant Classic!"). Both depend on the viewer knowing the original. The third way drops the quotation altogether and lets the copy carry the newness: Lazy Food names itself for the effort it saves and lets the pack talk.

Comfort and novelty are not in conflict here; they are in sequence. The quoted label supplies the comfort, the copy supplies the novelty, and the pack decides how far apart they sit. Sorry Nonna puts them one inch apart (the flavor name is the only new thing on the label). Lazy Food puts the whole pack on the novelty side and borrows comfort from the drawn pot alone.

tensions.title: Display type and label type

plates.caption: Yellowbird: display type as the whole pack.
Juicy Marbles: scale as hierarchy, grams small.
Heyday: the whole name in the instruction voice.

text: The heavy soft letter asks to be enjoyed; the condensed cap asks to be read. Nearly every pack on the board carries both, and the tension is one of proportion. Give the display type the panel and the pack is a toy; give the label type the panel and the pack is a specification. Juicy Marbles solves it by scale alone: one word enormous, the facts tiny, both in the same heavy grotesk. Heyday solves it by giving up the soft letter and letting color supply the pleasure.

The question underneath is who the pack thinks is looking: someone to be charmed or someone to be informed. The best packs on the board answer differently at two distances, charming across the aisle and informing in the hand.

tensions.title: Window and carton

plates.caption: The material: a clear sheet, seeds in it.
A pouch that shows the food.
A carton that tells about it.

text: Trust by sight or trust by voice. The translucent pouch and the die-cut window let the food prove itself; the printed carton has to describe it, and in exchange gets a surface to speak from. On this board the window pins are the beautiful ones (jelly, candy, rice in film) and the carton pins are the systematic ones (ranges, color per flavor, instruction rings).

The tension matters for a product whose wrapper is itself food and whose outer pack is a box. The board shows both halves separately and almost never together: a box with a window onto a translucent pouch exists on the board only as Nooma's pouch (045) and Brami's (274), and in neither is the thing seen through the window the interesting part.

tensions.title: Hero and family

plates.caption: One pack as a monument.
The range as a pattern.
The typology: nine cups, no pack.

text: A single pack on a field is a sculpture; a range tiled across the frame is a system. The board collects both, and brands tend to use one for the shelf and the other for the feed. The sculpture asks the pack to be beautiful alone, which favors heavy display type and the hard-lit set. The pattern asks the pack to be a unit, which favors color per flavor and a fixed frame.

The nine broth cups (184) are the extreme case: no pack at all, nine surfaces, and the arrangement is the whole image. It suggests a third option between hero and family, where the product's variety is the picture and the pack is implied.

tensions.title: Polished and naive

plates.caption: The rubber-hose cast: finish as craft.
One line, barely a face.
A naive character in a real cup.

text: Both are characters; they make opposite claims. The finished mascot says a studio made this and the brand has a history. The naive line says a person drew this and the brand is in on the joke. Neither is more sincere than the other; they are sincere about different things, craft and candor.

The pairing is interesting because the board's most-liked brand pins (Culture Cup, Long Weekend) sit at opposite ends, and both are soup-and-dessert categories where the character does the same job: it performs the food so that the photograph can stay simple.

tensions.title: Controlled set and real table

plates.caption: One hue over everything.
A lunch on a striped cloth.
Between the two: a real plate, a chosen palette.

text: The color-field set is the brand's room: everything in it was chosen to match the pack. The kitchen table is the buyer's room: the pack is one object among food and cloth. The first reads as control and therefore as brand; the second reads as life and therefore as trust.

The middle ground is the most used and the least examined: a real plate and real pickles on tile chosen to agree with the bottle (263). It is a set that pretends to be a table. Whether that pretense reads as warmth or as staging depends on how much of the room the pack is allowed to match.

brand_studies.name: Cometeer
brand_studies.sells: DTC flash-frozen coffee: a brewed puck in an aluminum capsule that melts into hot water, ice or milk.
brand_studies.effect: a near-future appliance brand with a 1960s warmth
synthesis: The product is something no one has seen, and the identity's job is to make the unfamiliar feel like an old favorite. The script wordmark does most of that: cream, connected, with a swash underline, it reads like a 1960s airline or a motel sign, which is the retro-future the studio named as its intent. Everything else on the box is the register of appliance packaging: small condensed caps, three icons, a ring of instruction ("melt, mix, enjoy") around the capsule.

Color is a sorting system and the only variable. One saturated hue per coffee, blue to red to pink to rust, with the photograph and the wordmark fixed, so a wall of boxes reads as a range of coffees rather than a range of designs. Each box also carries its roaster's own logo, which makes the system a frame around other brands.

The photograph is the argument. The capsule pours into an iced glass and a hot mug at once on the front; off the pack, the puck sinks in a glass mug in hard light, a hand tips a capsule, a bean sits in tweezers. These are demonstrations shot like jewelry, and together with the language ("Coffee from the near future") they make the brand the explanation of the product. The script keeps that explanation human.

brand_studies.name: Rose
brand_studies.sells: Flower-rosin cannabis edibles: sugared fruit cubes (Delights), chocolate, capsules and topicals, made with chefs and California farms.
formula: a flat box, one color per effect
a pattern taken from the food
cubes stacked on the thing they taste of
brand_studies.effect: a cannabis brand that reads as a chef's confectionery
synthesis: Rose is built like a restaurant, not a dispensary. The vocabulary is seasonal fruit, named chefs, farms, and the design follows: the box is a blank field in one color per effect (cream, orange, yellow, pink), with a small uneven "delights" mark and two lines of tiny caps. It behaves like a pastry box. The premium is carried by finish, emboss and spot gloss, and by fronts made from the food itself: raised white circles for boba, glossy seeds on matte red for watermelon. The pattern says ingredient before it says brand.

Photography stacks the cubes on the object that names the flavor or the effect, an apple, a melon, a clock, a cloud, in shallow focus against one color. The CGI renders of capsules and rosin extend the same idea toward science without leaving the pastry register. On screen the type is a grotesk and a Century, and the pages teach process rather than sell.
Together: minimal graphic surface, maximal material finish, food-first imagery. The brand's restraint is what makes a product most states regulate read as a thing from a good kitchen.

brand_studies.name: Stiller's
brand_studies.sells: Low-sugar soda in classic flavors: Lemon Lime, Root Beer, Shirley Temple, Shirley Cola.
formula: a metallic can, one color per flavor
an upright joined script running up the can
brand_studies.effect: the 1950s fountain sign reproduced exactly so the joke can be told straight
synthesis: The design is a pastiche with perfect fidelity. The joined script runs up the can like a wall sign; the can is metallic in one flavor color; the claims sit in navy bursts with white slab type ("Only 30 Calories!", "No Biotics!"); a boast in bold italic serif crosses the top. This is the grammar of mid-century soft-drink advertising, reproduced without irony on the can, so that the irony can live elsewhere.

Elsewhere is the copy and the film. "It's a soda for your mouth." "Made by 100% real human celebrity people." The celebrity founder is the punchline of his own brand, and the launch film parodies old soda ads. The imagery stays cold and literal: condensation beads, cans on a block of ice, a rope of root beer into a glass, each on a gradient of its own color.
Together: the straighter the can, the funnier the voice. A design that quoted loosely would have had to carry the joke itself; this one carries only the quotation, and the quotation is immaculate.

brand_studies.name: Sorry Nonna
brand_studies.sells: Australian jarred pasta sauce with rewritten classics: Spicy Gochujang, Zesty Limoncello, Creamy Vodka, Miso & Garlic.
formula: wide caps with an offset shadow
brand_studies.effect: a label that holds the straight face while the flavor name winks
synthesis: The label borrows the Italian tinned-tomato canon: bands, gold rules, wide display caps, primary colors, a brand line that wraps the jar ("We stole the recipe and made it better"). Everything on it is the tradition except one line, the flavor, and that line is the whole joke. Gochujang in an arrabbiata, limoncello in a marinara. The design never smiles, which is why the name can.

The system is one layout with a colorway per flavor and gold as the constant. Claims are red line icons on yellow discs inside a dashed ring, an angry nonna among them. The jar is photographed straight on against a gradient of its own label color, or in front of its own name set very large, or on gingham among older women cast as the nonnas. The site keeps the voice up ("Nonna would be appalled" in an empty cart).
Together: a brand in which the design is the authority and the copy is the rebellion, in equal measure, on every surface.

brand_studies.name: Alec's Culture Cup
brand_studies.sells: Single-serve probiotic ice cream under a crackable dark-chocolate shell, from Alec's Ice Cream (A2 dairy, regenerative farms).
formula: a brown soft serif larger than the parent name
one pastel per flavor, brown constant
a cast drawn in the flavor's darker tone
brand_studies.effect: a health product in the grammar of a treat
synthesis: The product has one action and the front shows it: the cup with its shell broken and a spoon going in. The sub-brand name, Culture Cup, is set larger than the parent in a brown soft serif with ball terminals, with "probiotic ice cream" arched over it, a cereal-box hierarchy. The parent's 2022 system is carried over underneath: the lowercase wordmark, a line-drawn cow and earth, a pastel per flavor.

Brown holds everything. It is the lettering, the shell and the constant across six pastels, so the range reads as one product in six flavors rather than six products. Characters drawn in each flavor's darker tone (cow, globe, sun) do the regenerative story without a paragraph; the numbers (140 calories, 10 g sugar) sit in corner tiles because the product is a portion and the portion is the promise.
Together: a health claim dressed as dessert. The shell is both the hero image and the reason brown can be the system's constant.

brand_studies.name: Wobble
brand_studies.sells: Gelatin dessert mix in a box: grass-fed gelatin, fruit juice powders, collagen. Strawberry, Sour Berry, Mango.
formula: a rounded lowercase wordmark laid over it
a narrow bouncy serif for titles
a maze on the side, stickers in the box
brand_studies.effect: a nostalgia product that does not look nostalgic in the old way
synthesis: The box front is a photograph of the molded jelly in its flavor color with the off-white rounded wordmark laid across it on a pale ground. The wordmark and the jelly share a silhouette, the mold, so the mark and the product become the same shape; the second logo lockup makes that literal by putting the word inside a red jelly-mold form. The retro references are carried by the type system rather than by texture: a narrow bouncy serif ("Friend") for titles, a soft rounded sans for subheads, a monoline script for asides, claims set in cut shapes that are themselves jelly molds.

Color is a named set of six, one per flavor plus accents, and the flavor color fills the field behind each box. The pack carries play on every panel, a maze on the side under "While you wait," four numbered steps on the back, a puffy sticker sheet and a jigsaw as extras, which is the positioning ("Play with your food") made into things.

Photography keeps to two scenes: jellies among toys in a flat lay, and one jelly on a cake stand with a cherry, both in soft even light. Together: a brand whose mark, product and claim shapes are all the same object, which is what lets it be bright without being loud.

possibilities: The product is a portion of food in a wrapper that is also food, dropped into a pot, sold in a box. Read against the board, three of the eighteen languages hold the most for it, and one is nearly absent.

Demonstration (L14) is the thinnest language on the board and the most important here. Cometeer shows what one brand can do when the photograph of the product's action is the identity. The drop into the pot and the dissolve have no equivalent on the board beyond those two coffee pins, which means the image is available.

Translucency (L16) is the only language that touches the product's material, and the material pins (331, 332, 177) are the closest the board comes to the wrapper itself. The tension with the carton (T4) is the product's own: a box that has to tell, around a pouch that can show.

The word in the food (L05) suits a product with one action to name. Lazy Nights and Dippa frame the dish with the name; TOMATO sets it on the sauce. For a name that is a verb, the type can be the frame and the pot can be inside it.

Heavy soft display type (L01), the character (L09) and the grocery vernacular (L15) are the board's crowd. They are where most of the pins are, and where most of the brands in the studies live. Which of them a new brand adopts is a choice about company, not about form.

names.rationale: A statement of magic, excitement and transformation.

names.name: Little Wonder
names.rationale: Celebrating the amazing metamorphosis that occurs all from one small pouch of delicious magic.

names.name: Hot Mess
names.rationale: Embracing the common slang expression to speak to the delicious mess that is a hot stew or soup and also the chaotic energy of our busy consumer.

names.name: Become
names.rationale: A transcendent and evocative expression for how the product transforms and becomes a delicious meal.

names.name: Mingle
names.rationale: The idea of ingredients getting together in a fun way that evokes social connection.

names.name: Smoosh
names.rationale: A fun word that speaks to the idea of the ingredients and packaging being integrated.

names.name: Cozy
names.rationale: Speaking to ingredients getting together in a way that relates to comfort food.

names.name: Cahoots
names.rationale: A fun expression for the way the ingredients and packaging are connected with eachother.

names.name: One
names.rationale: Very simply the ingredients and packaging are one unit that come together to deliver a singular culinary experience, perhaps for the singular busy consumer.

names.name: Caboodle
names.rationale: A shortening of ‘The Whole Kit and Caboodle’ to convey the idea of the entire package of contents and pouch being used. It’s also a whimsical word that rhymes with ‘noodle’.

names.name: Part & Parcel
names.rationale: Speaks to the entire package coming together to make the dish with a well-known piece of alliteration.

names.name: Pot Twist
names.rationale: Highlighting the key device used in the cooking ritual, but with a fun twist that relates to the innovative form.

names.name: Stir Crazy
names.rationale: A fun expression of the preparation process.

names.name: Goodie Bag
names.rationale: Speaks to a package of joy and deliciousness.

names.name: Pot Drop
names.rationale: Highlighting the key action of dropping the product in the pot with a memorable use of assonance.

names.name: Lickety
names.rationale: Speaking to the speed and convenience of the ritual (lickety split), with a whimsical word that also refers to deliciousness, i.e. licking.

names.name: Simma
names.rationale: A curious misspelling of the action to ‘simmer’.

names.name: Drop In
names.rationale: Speaking to the dropping of the product in the pot while also nodding to the idea of friends dropping in for a meal.
